OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify and diagnose midfoot arthritis via patient history and physical examination findings.
Identify signs of midfoot arthritis on imaging studies.
Review common treatment options for the management of midfoot arthritis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
The midfoot articulations include the naviculocuneiform and tarsometatarsal joints/cuboid
joints and the intertarsal joints.
Midfoot arthritis is a progressively painful and debilitating condition





Overview
Midfoot arthritis is a painful, debilitating condition that may affect young and old
patients. Often, it can be managed successfully via nonsurgical treatment options, such
as shoe modifications, anti-inflammatories, or orthotics. In patients with continued pain,
worsening deformity, or increasing disability, surgical treatment is considered.1
Epidemiology
Age distribution is bimodal.
Because midfoot arthritis can result from multiple etiologies, it may affect younger and older
patient populations.
Anatomy
The midfoot is the stable, load-transferring segment connecting the forefoot (metatarsals) to
the hindfoot (talus and calcaneus).
Osteology
Consists of three longitudinal columns: medial, middle, and lateral
Medial: medial cuneiform–first metatarsal
Middle: middle cuneiform–second metatarsal, lateral cuneiform–third metatarsal, and the
intercuneiform joints
Lateral: cuboid–fourth metatarsal and cuboid–fifth metatarsal

Osteology
The bony anatomy of the midfoot consists of three longitudinal columns: the medial,
middle, and lateral columns (Figure 1). These form a keystone or wedge-type
arrangement resembling a Roman arch that contributes to the stability of this portion of

the foot. The apex of this arch is the second metatarsal, which is recessed approximately
4 to 8 mm between the medial and middle cuneiforms.1
Figure 1
AP (A) and oblique (B) radiographs demonstrate the columnar anatomy of the midfoot.
(Reproduced from Yan AY, Hogan MV: Midfoot arthritis, in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 157-164.)
Joints and Ligaments
Dorsal, plantar, and intercuneiform ligaments provide added stability.
Intermetatarsal ligaments connect the bases of the second through fifth metatarsals.
The Lisfranc ligament is the largest ligament and runs obliquely from the medial cuneiform to
the base of the second metatarsal.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
3/20


Joints and Ligaments
The Lisfranc ligament consists of three ligaments: dorsal, plantar, and intraosseous. The
plantar component of the Lisfranc ligament connects the second and third metatarsals
with the medial cuneiform and is the strongest of the three.1 No ligament is present
between the first and second metatarsals.
Biomechanics
Motion at each joint varies.
The relationship between the Chopart joint and midfoot complex allows for load transfer from
the hindfoot to the forefoot.
The lateral column has more motion than the medial and middle columns.
The second and third tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints have been shown to bear the most load in
the midfoot.

Biomechanics
The motion of the navicular and cuboid bones at the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint
plays a considerable role in the gait cycle. If the axes of the talonavicular and
calcaneocuboid joints are parallel, the foot is flexible and acts as a shock absorber
during midstance. If the axes of these joints are not parallel, the foot becomes rigid and
acts as a lever for toe-off (Figure 2). The relationship between the Chopart joint and the
midfoot complex allows this load to transfer from the ankle and hindfoot into the
midfoot and forefoot. During supination-pronation, the cuboid-metatarsal joint has
approximately 10° of motion in the sagittal plane, whereas motion at the medial, middle,
and lateral cuneiform-metatarsal joints is 3.5°, 0.6°, and 1.6°, respectively. The second
and third TMT joints bear the load, and their relative stiffness is thought to be the reason
second and third TMT joint arthritis often is the most symptomatic.1 This lateral column
range of motion also is the reason lateral column stiffness (eg, after injury or surgical
arthrodesis) is so poorly tolerated.

Figure 2
Illustrations show the biomechanics of the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint. (Reproduced
with permission from Monk AP, Simpson DJ, Riley ND, Murray DW, Gill HS: Biomechanics
in orthopaedics: considerations of the lower limb. Surgery [Oxford] 2013;31[9]:445-451.)
Etiology
The etiology of midfoot arthritis may be primary, inflammatory/secondary, neuropathic, or
posttraumatic.
Posttraumatic arthritis of the midfoot is the most common type of midfoot arthritis followed
by primary arthritis and inflammatory or neuropathic changes.
Unmanaged TMT joint (Lisfranc) fracture-dislocation typically leads to loss of the longitudinal
arch and forefoot abduction.

Etiology
Midfoot arthritis may affect younger patients in their thirties with a history of trauma
and older patients in their fifties with primary arthritis. The trauma most associated with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
5/20

the development of midfoot arthritis is a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation. Although the rate
of midfoot fracture-dislocations is approximately 0.2%, these injuries are missed in 20%
of patients.1
Risk Factors
Pes planus
First ray instability
Short first metatarsal
Long second metatarsal
History of midfoot fracture-dislocation

Risk Factors
Patients with chronic pes planus, first ray instability, a short first metatarsal, or a long
second metatarsal may be predisposed to deformity and arthritis at the midfoot.
Common midfoot arthritis deformities are forefoot abduction, collapse of the
longitudinal arch, and hindfoot valgus. If the longitudinal arch collapses, plantar tension
increases, which compromises midfoot lever function during gait. Injury, degeneration,
inflammation, and deformity may cause progressive articular cartilage damage and loss
of bony and soft-tissue integrity that results in painful midfoot arthritis.1
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients report dorsal midfoot or arch pain with weight bearing, particularly with push-off
during gait.
May also report irritation of the deep peroneal nerve because of osteophytes or ganglion cysts

Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
6/20

The most common symptom patients report is pain in the midtarsal region with loading.
They note that this pain may severely restrict their ability to walk and perform activities
of daily living. Pain often is worse with forced plantar flexion, such as during ascension of
stairs. Patients also may report a deep pain that is present at rest. Dorsal prominences
and osteophytes can develop and cause problems with wearing closed shoes.1
Physical Examination
Pain is elicited via palpation or stress, such as with the pronation/abduction stress test.
Dorsal osteophytes may interfere with shoe wear.
Loss of the longitudinal arch
Secondary hindfoot valgus, Achilles tendon contracture, and hallux valgus also may be
present.

Physical Examination
Loss of the longitudinal arch (occasionally associated with forefoot abduction) is
frequently observed with weight bearing and evident on radiographs. Midfoot arthritis is
the second most common cause of longitudinal arch loss after posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction. During the physical examination, attention should be paid to the alignment
of the foot while standing to assess for any deformity in the sagittal or coronal planes.
Physical examination maneuvers to elicit the area of maximum pain include the piano
key test and the abduction-pronation stress test. In the piano key test, individual distal
metatarsal heads are pressed down, and pain in the midfoot is noted.2 The Coleman
block test and the Silfverskiöld test should be performed if any deformity is present and
can be used for decision-making in surgical management is necessary.1
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standing AP, oblique, and lateral radiographs are necessary.

Similar to other types of arthritis, joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and dorsal
foot osteophytes are observed in affected joints.
Weight-bearing radiographs of the foot demonstrate a nonlinear talus–first metatarsal
relationship, with the apex of the deformity at the midfoot and loss of medial cuneiform
height (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Radiographs of the foot and ankle of a patient with midfoot arthritis. Preoperative
AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate midfoot arthritis with deformity. AP (C) and
lateral (D) radiographs obtained after midfoot fusion with realignment. (Reproduced from
Adams SB, Easley ME: Arthritides of the foot and ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1167-1181.)
Standing radiographs are obtained to identify the location and extent of the disease and to
identify any deformity. Radiographs may demonstrate a lower medial cuneiform and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
8/20

negative talus–first metatarsal angle (Meary angle) in patients with primary arthritis,
dissimilar from radiographs of patients with traumatic midfoot arthritis.1 Radiographs may
indicate prior, even subtle, Lisfranc subluxation.
CT may be useful if symptomatic disease is not observed on plain radiographs
Weight-bearing CT scans, if available, have a role in revealing joint degeneration and
deformity.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
NSAIDs
Activity modifications
Orthotics
Shoe modifications
Fluoroscopic-guided or ultrasonographic-guided corticosteroid injections are diagnostic and
potentially therapeutic.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is the initial treatment option for patients with midfoot
arthritis. The goal is to offload and stabilize the midfoot. This can be achieved via activity
and shoe modifications, orthotics, anti-inflammatories and local corticosteroid and
anesthetic injections. Shoe modifications include stiff-soled shoes and rocker-bottom
shoes (Figure 4). Orthotics that are stiff or carbon fiber inserts may help support the
arch and midfoot. A 2009 study showed that wearing full-length carbon-graphite inserts
for 4 weeks resulted in improvement in midfoot arthritis symptoms.3 Injections of
corticosteroid with or without local anesthetic have not afforded long-term pain relief.
Studies have shown that patients can achieve temporary pain relief with these injections
(mean 3-month duration); however, they may be useful in identifying joints that are
symptomatic.1,4,5

Figure 4 Photograph shows a rocker-bottom shoe. (Courtesy of Joan Ryan Williams, MD,
San Diego, CA.)
Surgical Management
Near-full physiologic foot function, particularly during push-off, can be reestablished via
successful realignment and arthrodesis of the first through third TMT and/or
naviculocuneiform joints (Figure 5).
Figure 5 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of a foot demonstrate medial and middle column
arthrodesis for the management of abduction deformity, sagittal midfoot collapse, and
midfoot arthritis. (Courtesy of Bruce E. Cohen, MD, Charlotte, NC.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
10/20

Internal fixation of the midfoot articulations has evolved to include screws, staples, and plates
specifically indicated for midfoot arthrodesis.
Lateral column arthrodesis typically is not recommended because of increased mobility.

Surgical Management
The mainstay of surgical management of medial and middle column arthritis is
arthrodesis of the affected joints. If more than 2 mm of displacement or more than 15°
of deformity is present, the joints need to be realigned before fusion.1 Most often, the
medial and middle columns are fused; however, if instability remains, the intercuneiform
or naviculocuneiform joints also can be fused. A few studies have reported a union rate
higher than 90% and patient satisfaction with fusion.6 Management of any deformity at
the joint is important because achieving anatomic reduction is the most important
predictor of a good outcome.
Fusion of the lateral column rarely is performed. Because of increased mobility at the
lateral column, arthrodesis typically is avoided because it may lead to stress fractures,
nonunion, a rigid prominence, and additional pain. Resection arthroplasty and
interpositional arthroplasty are alternatives to fusion at the fourth and fifth TMT joints.
Interposition arthroplasty of the fourth and fifth TMT joints results in approximately 50%
reduction in pain and is associated with the potential for subsidence or dislocation of the
implant.7 Berlet et al8 reported a 35% decrease in pain and maintenance of lateral
column motion in 12 patients who underwent interpositional arthroplasty with use of
the peroneus tertius tendon. Ceramic spherical interpositional arthroplasty was an
alternative. Shawen et al9 eported an 87% improvement in American Orthopaedic Foot
and Ankle Society scores and pain improvement of 42% at 34-month follow-up in 11
patients who underwent ceramic spherical interpositional arthroplasty of the fourth or
fifth TMT joints.1
Indications
Patients who have failed to respond to 6 months of nonsurgical treatment

Primary arthrodesis in Lisfranc injuries

Indications
Surgical management of symptomatic midfoot arthritis is indicated after 6 months of
failed nonsurgical management; however, some patients should undergo primary
arthrodesis for the management of Lisfranc injuries. This often is advocated in patients
with ligamentous injuries because ligament healing is less predictable than direct bony
healing and in patients with substantially comminuted Lisfranc fracture-dislocations.
Contraindications
Contraindications to interposition arthroplasty are active infection or insufficient bone to
contain the interposition.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Implants include cannulated and solid screws ranging from 2.7 to 4.5 mm.
Wide range of plating systems for dorsal, medial or plantar plating
Evaluate need for additional osteotomies or soft-tissue balancing for realignment

Preoperative Planning
Various plate configurations and plating systems are available, including medial, dorsal,
or plantar plating, use of a single plate on each joint, or use of one plate to cover
multiple articulations and facilitate fusion across multiple joints. Screws can be fully
threaded and used in a lag fashion or partially threaded and used for compression.
Realignment procedures often consist of osteotomies and soft-tissue balancing.
Orthobiologics from autogenic and allogenic sources have been used to fill bony defects
and to promote bone healing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
12/20

Patient Positioning
Supine
Surgical Approaches
Most common approach is one or two dorsal longitudinal incisions with care to maintain
adequate skin bridges for medial and middle column arthrodesis.
Medial midline approach can be used for considerable medial column collapse, for which
corrective osteotomy and plantar plating are planned.
To access the lateral column, incision can be made dorsally between the fourth and fifth
metatarsals.

Surgical Approaches
The incisions for midfoot arthrodesis depend on the joints being fused. A single incision
in line with the second metatarsal is commonly used. This approach releases the
extensor hallucis brevis and exposes the deep neurovascular bundle, which can be
mobilized medially or laterally to access the first, second, and third TMT joints. If a
surgeon prefers a two-incision approach, the first incision typically is made between the
first and second metatarsals, which will provide access to the first TMT joint and a large
portion of the second TMT joint (Figure 6). Care must be taken to protect the superficial
and deep peroneal nerves and the dorsalis pedis artery. The incision should be just
lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, which is medial to the neurovascular
bundle (Figure 7). Deeper dissection is then carried out between the extensor hallucis
longus and the extensor hallucis brevis, protecting the neurovascular bundle lateral to
the extensor hallucis brevis. To address the third TMT joint, a second incision is centered
over the third metatarsal.10

Postoperative Management
Non–weight bearing in a splint or cast for the first 2 weeks postoperatively
Sutures can be removed 10 to 14 days postoperatively.
After cast removal, can transition to a controlled ankle motion orthosis for 4 to 6 weeks
If radiographs obtained 6 to 8 weeks postoperatively demonstrate adequate healing, partial–
weight bearing is allowed followed by a transition to full–weight bearing.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Arthritides of the Midfoot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
15/20

Select patients with symptomatic fourth and fifth TMT joint arthritis may be treated via
interposition arthroplasty, which maintains the lateral column and accommodates gait.
TMT joints are 2 to 3 cm deep; complete joint preparation must extend to the plantar surface
to optimize physiologic alignment and fusion.
Care must be taken to not malposition the second and third TMT joints during arthrodesis.
Excessive plantar flexion will cause metatarsalgia of the involved ray, and excessive
dorsiflexion will cause transfer metatarsalgia of the adjacent rays.
Severe deformity may warrant a biplanar midfoot osteotomy in combination with arthrodesis,
particularly in patients with a non-braceable Charcot midfoot deformity.
Given the high prevalence of midfoot arthritis after Lisfranc injury, primary arthrodesis may be
considered, especially in patients with associated metatarsal base fractures.
Surgical management of midfoot arthritis may warrant simultaneous Achilles tendon
lengthening and hindfoot realignment.

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
In fusing the medial and middle columns, protection of the superficial sensory nerves is
important because they can form painful neuromas if injured. In addition, the dorsalis
pedis artery goes from dorsal to plantar between the first and second metatarsals;
therefore, care should be taken during the placement of screws and during dissection in
that area. If a two-incision approach is used, a skin bridge of at least 4 cm should be left
between the incisions to prevent wound-healing complications. The first TMT joint is 30
mm deep. Care must be taken to attain adequate expose so all cartilage can be
removed. If exposure is inadequate, the joint often is fused with the first metatarsal in
dorsiflexion.10
Complications
Infection (3%)
Peripheral nerve injury (9%)
Painful neuroma formation (7%)
Nonunion (3% to 7%)
Implant complications (9%)
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004003
16/20

Stress fracture (7%)
Metatarsalgia (6%)
Sesamoid pain (8%)
Sural nerve neuralgia (7.5%)
Secondary arthritis in adjacent joints
Complex regional pain syndrome

Complications
Complications associated with midfoot arthrodesis include infection, peripheral nerve
injury that may result in a painful neuroma, nonunion, implant complications,
metatarsalgia, and adjacent joint arthritis. Elderly patients have a higher risk for
nonunion.
Outcomes
Arthrodesis may result in substantial improvement in pain, disability, and activity limitations.
A 2011 study reported that midfoot arthrodesis for the management of primary arthritis was
associated with a 90% satisfaction rate.6
Nonunion is the most common complication associated with patient dissatisfaction and poor
outcomes.

Outcomes
A 2012 study reported a 93% fusion rate of the medial and middle columns with the use
of a hybrid plate with locking and nonlocking screws.11 Ahmad et al12 compared plate-
and-screw constructs versus screw constructs reported that both constructs can
improve function and pain; however, plate-and-screw constructs may result in a higher
rate of bony healing.1
